lessons.practical_assignment: Complete Gate G with an integration test, synthesis report and short demonstration. Pass: another person reruns the simulation, all timing assumptions are listed and any physical measurements are distinguished from modeled estimates.
lessons.assigned_reading: R32-R34: repeatable simulation and synthesis; R15: system integration; handbook safety review for physical extensions.

volumes.title: Gaming Platforms and Hardware/Software Co-design
volumes.purpose: Study boards, memory, GPU architecture, performance, input/display pipelines and integrated design.

modules.title: Embedded platforms, drivers and board design
modules.prerequisites: Modules 17-18 and 31-35. Physical work remains optional and supervised.
modules.project: Design a simulated controller or peripheral with firmware, a host interface and a schematic-level review. A physical board extension begins only after the electrical, layout and bring-up plans receive qualified review.

lessons.title: Serial interfaces and peripheral contracts
lessons.outcome: Choose a communication interface using timing and electrical constraints.
lessons.practical_assignment: Build a simulated peripheral transaction decoder and driver for one interface. Pass: incorrect framing or mode is detected, timeouts are bounded and a complete interface-contract table is provided.
lessons.assigned_reading: R53: device drivers, UART, SPI and I2C APIs; R51: bus-level driver documentation. For hardware, add the exact peripheral datasheet.

lessons.title: Firmware, RTOS scheduling and driver lifecycle
lessons.outcome: Bound embedded work and make device state transitions explicit.
lessons.practical_assignment: Use a supported RTOS simulator or a deterministic scheduler model to implement input, processing and logging tasks. Pass: deadlines are evaluated under injected load and removal/cancellation leaves no live invalid requests.
lessons.assigned_reading: R53: kernel scheduling, synchronization and device model; R51: driver lifecycle and power management.

lessons.title: Schematics, PCB layout, power integrity and signal integrity
lessons.outcome: Translate a circuit into a manufacturable layout without ignoring physics.
lessons.practical_assignment: Create a low-speed peripheral schematic and unrouted or simple two-layer layout in KiCad. Pass: footprints are checked against datasheets, ERC/DRC findings are resolved or justified and a reviewer inspects power and return paths before fabrication.
lessons.assigned_reading: R36: schematic editor, PCB editor, ERC and DRC; R30: nonideal circuit behavior; R49: interconnect and packaging extension.

lessons.title: Bring-up, instrumentation and fault isolation
lessons.outcome: Turn an unresponsive device into a sequence of testable hypotheses.
lessons.practical_assignment: Write and rehearse a bring-up procedure against a simulated device with injected clock, reset and protocol faults. Pass: each fault has a safe diagnostic branch and the procedure includes explicit stop conditions.
lessons.assigned_reading: R53: board support and debugging; R36: fabrication outputs and design review; selected instrument manuals for any physical extension.

modules.title: GPU microarchitecture and memory systems
modules.project: Create a GPU architecture workbook connecting shader behavior to execution groups, registers, memory transactions and fixed-function resources. Measure one accessible GPU or clearly label a simulator-only study.

lessons.title: SIMT execution, divergence, occupancy and latency hiding
lessons.outcome: Explain why many threads do not guarantee useful parallel work.
lessons.practical_assignment: Compare coherent and divergent workloads, varying register pressure or group size where supported. Pass: outputs agree, device group assumptions are recorded and the report does not equate occupancy with performance.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: programming model, execution and hardware implementation; R48: vector and multithreaded architecture foundations.

lessons.title: Coalescing, local storage, caches and shared-memory banks
lessons.outcome: Match data layout to the memory transactions actually performed.
lessons.practical_assignment: Benchmark contiguous, strided and tiled access with identical useful work. Pass: count useful bytes, state the relevant memory level and include any layout-conversion cost in the application comparison.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: device memory access, shared memory and performance considerations; R43: operational intensity.

lessons.title: Raster, texture, matrix and ray-tracing units
lessons.outcome: Understand fixed-function acceleration as specialized tradeoffs.
lessons.practical_assignment: Analyze one texture-heavy, arithmetic-heavy or ray-query workload. Pass: identify the likely resource limits using measurements or a documented model and state supported precision and feature assumptions.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: architecture and specialized operations; R21: graphics/compute capabilities; R23: ray intersection and acceleration reference.

lessons.title: CPU-GPU sharing, discrete memory and synchronization
lessons.outcome: Treat shared addressability separately from ownership and cost.
lessons.practical_assignment: Compare an upload/compute/readback path with an available shared-memory path, or model both with stated assumptions. Pass: correct ownership, separate phase timings and no claim that unified means zero-cost.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: memory management and synchronization; R21, R24 or R25: the selected platform's resource-sharing contract.

modules.title: Quantitative performance engineering
modules.project: Produce a performance investigation with a hypothesis, controlled workload, raw measurements, uncertainty, a bottleneck model and a verified optimization. A negative result is acceptable when the evidence is rigorous.

lessons.title: Amdahl, roofline and bottleneck models
lessons.outcome: Use upper bounds to reject implausible optimization claims.
lessons.practical_assignment: Build a roofline worksheet for one kernel and an Amdahl estimate for one frame optimization. Pass: units cancel correctly, modeled ceilings use the declared memory level and observed deviations are explained as hypotheses.
lessons.assigned_reading: R43: original Roofline model; R48: quantitative architecture; revisit Module 18 parallel limits.

lessons.title: Profilers, counters and trustworthy benchmark design
lessons.outcome: Distinguish observation from an explanation that still needs testing.
lessons.practical_assignment: Create a benchmark harness with warmup, repeated runs, output validation and metadata. Pass: an intentional no-op or wrong-result variant is rejected and all included/excluded samples are documented.
lessons.assigned_reading: R26: profiling; R37: performance analysis; R09: inference and uncertainty.

lessons.title: SIMD, cache blocking, NUMA and job scheduling
lessons.outcome: Optimize locality and parallelism together.
lessons.practical_assignment: Optimize a particle or transform workload using one locality change and one scheduling change. Pass: test tail sizes, report numerical differences, and measure small as well as large workloads to expose overhead.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: parallel memory patterns; R48: multiprocessors and memory systems; R11: safe C++ and concurrency.

lessons.title: Energy, thermal behavior and sustained performance
lessons.outcome: Evaluate useful work over time rather than only a short peak.
lessons.practical_assignment: Run a sustained workload within normal device limits or analyze a synthetic power trace. Pass: distinguish watts from joules, report the measurement boundary and compare early versus sustained performance.
lessons.assigned_reading: R48: quantitative architecture; R51: device power management; R37: GPU execution and performance context.

modules.title: Gaming-platform constraints and interactive latency
modules.project: Create a platform capability and latency report for the engine. Implement one non-desktop constraint in simulation or on an available device: touch input, suspend/resume, restricted memory, variable presentation or XR timing.

lessons.title: Input-to-display latency and frame pacing
lessons.outcome: Account for the whole interaction path rather than only frame rate.
lessons.practical_assignment: Instrument input receipt, simulation consumption, render submission and presentation-related timestamps. Pass: explain which stages are actually measured and which remain estimated, and show a frame-pacing distribution.
lessons.assigned_reading: R22: input and event timing; R24 or R25: presentation; R52: frame timing as an advanced comparison.

lessons.title: Mobile and handheld systems: memory, power and lifecycle
lessons.outcome: Design for suspension, limited budgets and sustained use.
lessons.practical_assignment: Add suspend/resume simulation and a constrained memory mode. Pass: progress survives the documented lifecycle, resources are restored safely and quality changes do not alter authoritative simulation rules.
lessons.assigned_reading: R25: platform graphics resources; R22: application lifecycle events; R29: text and input usability; R51: power-management concepts.

lessons.title: XR spaces, stereo views, pose timing and comfort constraints
lessons.outcome: Render from runtime-provided timing and coordinate contracts.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement two simulated camera views and a pose-time log, or a minimal OpenXR scene on available supported hardware. Pass: spaces and units are explicit, frame timing follows the runtime and loss of tracking has defined behavior.
lessons.assigned_reading: R52: spaces, view configuration, frame loop and timing; R29: interaction and accessibility review.

lessons.title: Portability, platform services and console-development boundaries
lessons.outcome: Build transferable systems without assuming proprietary access.
lessons.practical_assignment: Write a platform interface and capability matrix, then implement a second backend or strict mock. Pass: assumptions about paths, input and lifecycle are exposed, and proprietary requirements are marked unavailable until authorized.
lessons.assigned_reading: R22, R24 and R25: platform interfaces; R29: cross-device usability; official authorized platform documentation only for restricted targets.

modules.title: Hardware/software co-design capstone
modules.project: Gate H: choose one game workload and compare a software baseline with a specialized hardware or architecture alternative. Deliver a reference implementation, model or RTL, software interface, verification evidence and an end-to-end tradeoff report.

lessons.title: Workload characterization and measurable requirements
lessons.outcome: Derive hardware goals from a real software operation.
lessons.practical_assignment: Select a workload from the engine and write a requirement sheet plus baseline measurements. Pass: each target has units and a test, and the maximum plausible application benefit is estimated.
lessons.assigned_reading: R43: bottleneck modeling; R48: quantitative design; R49: project methodology.

lessons.title: Architecture alternatives, arithmetic precision and dataflow
lessons.outcome: Explore several designs before committing to one.
lessons.practical_assignment: Model three variants, such as scalar, pipelined and multi-lane. Pass: resource and bandwidth estimates are explicit, fixed-point error meets a chosen application tolerance and rejected variants have documented reasons.
lessons.assigned_reading: R49: architecture and RTL modeling; R43: bandwidth limits; R33: resource inference.

lessons.title: Interface design, virtualization and end-to-end evaluation
lessons.outcome: Include the host software in the hardware result.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement a host driver model with invalid-descriptor, timeout and reset tests. Pass: buffer bounds are enforced, ownership survives failure and results include both kernel and end-to-end timing.
lessons.assigned_reading: R51: DMA and device interfaces; R49: system integration; R38: modeled systems when hardware is unavailable.

lessons.title: Design review, evidence tiers and undergraduate CE completion
lessons.outcome: Defend a co-design decision with limitations and reproducible artifacts.
lessons.practical_assignment: Complete Gate H and a design-review presentation. Pass: every major claim traces to an artifact, the baseline is reproduced and a limitations section clearly separates educational estimates from production claims.
lessons.assigned_reading: R49: design-project reporting; R48: architectural tradeoffs; revisit the evidence and project rubrics in the handbook.

volumes.title: Graduate Game-Engine and Graphics Engineering
volumes.purpose: Derive algorithms, reproduce research, optimize parallel systems and defend measured engineering choices.

modules.title: Graduate numerical methods and research practice
modules.prerequisites: Gates B, F and H; rigorous linear algebra, calculus, probability and systems competence.
modules.project: Produce a graduate numerical notebook with derivations, reference implementations, conditioning experiments and a preregistered evaluation plan. Complete substantial assigned problem sets; the short lesson quizzes are only formative checks.

lessons.title: Reading research as claims, assumptions and evidence
lessons.outcome: Extract an implementable argument rather than only a paper summary.
lessons.practical_assignment: Analyze one paper associated with R23, R44 or R55. Pass: a two-page claim map, a reconstructed central algorithm, at least three assumptions and a feasible reproduction target are reviewed by another reader.
lessons.assigned_reading: R23: Further Reading sections for a chosen rendering topic; R44 or R55: one named original paper; handbook research-reading template.

lessons.title: Conditioning, sparse systems and iterative solvers
lessons.outcome: Choose a solver from mathematical properties and error requirements.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement a sparse matrix-vector product and conjugate gradient for a verified SPD system. Pass: derive the relevant assumptions, compare residual and forward error, and evaluate a simple preconditioner over several conditioning levels.
lessons.assigned_reading: R54: linear systems, positive definiteness and numerical methods; R07: orthogonality and eigenvalues; R42: numerical optimization background.

lessons.title: Constrained optimization, derivatives and optimality conditions
lessons.outcome: Derive and verify an optimization method for an engineering objective.
lessons.practical_assignment: Derive the example, then solve a constrained fitting or IK problem with a numerical method. Pass: derivative checks, feasibility residual, convergence criteria and at least one failure or sensitivity case are reported.
lessons.assigned_reading: R42: convexity, duality, optimality and numerical methods; R41: gradients and constrained differentials.

lessons.title: Experimental design, uncertainty and reproducible graduate work
lessons.outcome: Make a performance or quality claim that survives independent scrutiny.
lessons.practical_assignment: Preregister a small experiment with baseline, primary metric, trial unit and exclusion policy. Pass: raw data and analysis scripts reproduce the tables, and an ablation isolates at least one proposed mechanism.
lessons.assigned_reading: R09: statistical inference; R42: experimental examples; handbook benchmark and research templates.

modules.title: Advanced parallel and GPU algorithms
modules.project: Implement a reusable GPU reduction, scan or compaction primitive and integrate it into an engine workload. Compare a simple reference, a competent library baseline when available and your implementation at equal correctness requirements.

lessons.title: Parallel reductions, scans and work-span analysis
lessons.outcome: Prove the structure of a parallel primitive before tuning it.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement reduction and either scan or compaction. Pass: derive work/span bounds, test sizes 0, 1 and non-powers of two, and report the numerical/reproducibility contract.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: cooperative execution and synchronization; R48: parallel architectures; derive algorithm bounds using Module 14 methods.

lessons.title: Tiling, data reuse and asynchronous pipelines
lessons.outcome: Overlap movement and computation without creating races.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement a tiled matrix multiply or image filter, then one overlap variant where supported. Pass: adversarial dimensions match the reference, synchronization is checked and the end-to-end comparison includes staging overhead.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: shared memory, synchronization and asynchronous operations where supported; R43: operational intensity.

lessons.title: Irregular workloads, wavefront scheduling and load balance
lessons.outcome: Design around variable work rather than assuming identical threads.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement an irregular workload using static assignment and a queue or compaction alternative. Pass: prove or test termination, handle queue capacity safely and measure tail behavior as well as mean throughput.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: execution, atomics and synchronization; R48: multithreaded scheduling; R23: wavefront rendering as an application.

lessons.title: Portable performance and integration-quality evaluation
lessons.outcome: Separate algorithmic benefit from one device-specific tuning win.
lessons.practical_assignment: Integrate the selected primitive into the engine and evaluate at least two workload regimes. Pass: application impact is measured, unsupported features fall back safely and any untested device claims are explicitly excluded.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37 and R21: capability contracts; R43: performance models; Module 41 experimental protocol.

modules.title: Advanced rendering and reconstruction
modules.project: Reproduce a bounded rendering result and add one justified extension. Derive the estimator or reconstruction objective, compare equal-quality cost, include temporal failure cases and preserve source scenes and evaluation scripts.

lessons.title: Monte Carlo light transport and multiple importance sampling
lessons.outcome: Derive estimators with correct densities and measures.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement a path tracer with explicit light sampling and MIS. Pass: derive the estimator, verify a simple known integral, compare variance at equal cost and test emission and grazing-angle edge cases.
lessons.assigned_reading: R23: Monte Carlo Integration, Light Transport and sampling strategies. Work the associated mathematical exercises, not only the implementation.

lessons.title: Real-time ray tracing, dynamic acceleration and hybrid pipelines
lessons.outcome: Budget traversal, building and shading as one system.
lessons.practical_assignment: Add one ray-traced effect to the engine or build a software hybrid prototype. Pass: dynamic-scene tests include total update cost, missing-information fallbacks and resource synchronization evidence.
lessons.assigned_reading: R23: intersection acceleration and light transport; R21, R24 or R25: supported ray-tracing interfaces for an optional hardware route.

lessons.title: Spatiotemporal reuse, reservoirs and denoising
lessons.outcome: Evaluate variance reduction together with bias, history validity and motion.
lessons.practical_assignment: Reproduce a small weighted-reservoir example or temporal denoiser, then evaluate on motion and disocclusion sequences. Pass: the selection/weight rule is derived, bias limitations are stated and results include sequence-level failure cases.
lessons.assigned_reading: R44: original ReSTIR paper and its estimator assumptions; R23: sampling theory; read only the selected bounded method before expanding scope.

lessons.title: Differentiable and neural rendering under engineering constraints
lessons.outcome: Test learned or gradient-based methods against explicit baselines.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement a small inverse-rendering optimization or learned reconstruction experiment. Pass: gradient or generalization checks, a non-learned baseline, compute/memory accounting and a distribution-shift failure analysis are included.
lessons.assigned_reading: R47: automatic differentiation, optimization and generalization; R23: light transport and sampling foundations; select one original method with Module 41's paper-review protocol.

modules.title: Advanced engine systems and simulation research
modules.project: Conduct an engine-system experiment with a formal model or numerical argument, a reference implementation and stress-tested integration. Choose one main depth area: world streaming, simulation, distributed state or reliability.

lessons.title: Large-world scheduling, streaming and critical-path control
lessons.outcome: Design a bounded system under changing content and workload.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement a bounded world-streaming scheduler or large-coordinate experiment. Pass: teleport and memory-pressure tests preserve correctness, peak resources are measured and the critical path is explained with a trace.
lessons.assigned_reading: R26: world, task and streaming systems for comparison; R20: engine architecture; R54: numerical conditioning where coordinate precision is studied.

lessons.title: Deformable simulation, variational models and solver tradeoffs
lessons.outcome: Derive a physical or constraint model before comparing visual results.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement a small cloth, elastic bar or compliant-constraint model and compare two integration/solver choices. Pass: derive the core equations, check gradients, quantify constraint or energy error and reproduce one bounded result from the assigned research.
lessons.assigned_reading: R54: equilibrium, variational and differential-equation methods; R55: 2016 XPBD and related position-based simulation course notes.

lessons.title: Distributed game state, consistency and overload behavior
lessons.outcome: Specify which guarantees survive network delay and partial failure.
lessons.practical_assignment: Model a two-partition entity handoff with injected failure. Pass: a stated safety invariant holds, recovery assumptions are explicit and overload is bounded without unbounded retry amplification.
lessons.assigned_reading: R17-R18: transport and transactions; R20: game-state architecture; use Module 41's claim and experiment discipline for the distributed model.

lessons.title: Formal specifications, replay and reliability-oriented engine design
lessons.outcome: Use precise invariants to reduce the space of subtle failures.
lessons.practical_assignment: Model a small engine lifecycle or queue protocol and connect it to implementation tests. Pass: at least one safety and one conditional liveness property are defined, a deliberate violation is found and abstraction limits are documented.
lessons.assigned_reading: R50: safety, liveness and assumptions as a formal-methods reference; R11 and Module 18: ownership/concurrency contracts; R26: system comparison.

modules.title: Compilers, shader languages and engine specialization
modules.project: Gate I: deliver a research-quality reproduction and extension in rendering, simulation, GPU algorithms or compilation. This module also requires a small compiler optimization with semantic tests, generated-code inspection and end-to-end measurements.

lessons.title: Intermediate representations, SSA and dataflow analysis
lessons.outcome: Represent program meaning so transformations can be justified.
lessons.practical_assignment: Extend the tiny compiler with a control-flow IR and one dataflow analysis. Pass: derive transfer functions and a fixed-point stopping condition, test loops and merges, and verify transformed programs against an interpreter.
lessons.assigned_reading: R14: LLVM frontend, control flow and optimization tutorials; R48: compiler/architecture interaction.

lessons.title: Alias analysis, vectorization and legal optimization
lessons.outcome: Separate transformations that are fast from transformations that preserve meaning.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement or study a loop transformation with an explicit legality check. Pass: overlapping-memory and boundary cases are tested, compiler flags are recorded and speed claims exclude transformations that violate the required numerical contract.
lessons.assigned_reading: R14: optimization and code generation; R11: aliasing, lifetime and arithmetic guidance; R37: vector/parallel execution consequences.

lessons.title: Domain-specific languages, specialization and safe JIT execution
lessons.outcome: Trade generality for predictable game-engine computation.
lessons.practical_assignment: Build a typed expression or material DSL with constant folding and a bounded interpreter or JIT route. Pass: invalid graphs fail safely, variant counts are measured and compiled outputs match the reference.
lessons.assigned_reading: R14: language implementation and JIT; R26: material and scripting concepts for comparison; Module 20: trust boundaries.

lessons.title: Compiler/hardware co-design and graduate artifact review
lessons.outcome: Connect a transformation to architecture and application evidence.
lessons.practical_assignment: Complete Gate I and defend one compiler transformation's legality. Pass: an independent reader reruns the central experiment, the claimed extension is precisely identified and raw evidence supports the conclusions.
lessons.assigned_reading: R14 and R48: compilation and architecture; R49: co-design methodology; Module 41: research evaluation protocol.

volumes.title: Graduate Gaming Hardware and Research Thesis
volumes.purpose: Evaluate advanced architectures, physical design and verification, then complete and defend a research artifact.

modules.title: Advanced computer architecture for gaming workloads
modules.project: Perform an architecture study using a pinned simulator or a carefully bounded analytical model. Compare at least three configurations on representative and adverse game-related workloads, and validate the model against a known reference where possible.

lessons.title: Cache coherence, memory consistency and synchronization
lessons.outcome: Separate agreement about a location from ordering across locations.
lessons.practical_assignment: Model a small coherence protocol and evaluate message-passing litmus tests under stated language and hardware models. Pass: ownership invariants hold, transient races are considered and coherence is not confused with data-race freedom.
lessons.assigned_reading: R48: multiprocessors, coherence and consistency; R35: selected memory-ordering specification; R11: language-level concurrency.

lessons.title: Out-of-order execution, speculation and precise state
lessons.outcome: Increase instruction overlap without changing architectural outcomes.
lessons.practical_assignment: Use a simulator or detailed scheduling model to compare in-order and out-of-order execution on independent and dependent instruction streams. Pass: architectural results agree and bottleneck explanations include true dependencies and resource limits.
lessons.assigned_reading: R48: superscalar, out-of-order, prediction and exception handling; R38: CPU models and configuration.

lessons.title: Architecture simulation, traces and model validation
lessons.outcome: Use simulation as evidence with a stated fidelity boundary.
lessons.practical_assignment: Run a cache, scheduling or accelerator study with at least one validation case and a sensitivity sweep. Pass: raw configurations reproduce results, modeled versus measured quantities are labeled and conclusions do not exceed the tested fidelity.
lessons.assigned_reading: R38: simulation models, statistics and configuration; R48: architecture evaluation; R43: analytical bounds.

lessons.title: Memory systems, chiplets and multi-objective design
lessons.outcome: Choose an architecture across performance, power, cost and complexity.
lessons.practical_assignment: Construct a Pareto comparison of at least three architecture configurations. Pass: objectives and assumptions are explicit, dominated designs are identified correctly and a recommendation changes appropriately when a hard constraint changes.
lessons.assigned_reading: R48: memory and quantitative design; R49: packaging and system tradeoffs; R38: architecture alternatives.

modules.title: VLSI, timing and physical implementation
modules.prerequisites: Modules 31-34, 40 and 46. Use educational libraries and licensed or open tools only.
modules.project: Carry a verified small RTL block through an educational synthesis and physical-design flow. Report constraints, timing, area and power-estimation assumptions. The result is a learning artifact, not fabrication-ready commercial signoff.

lessons.title: CMOS logic, transistor sizing and delay models
lessons.outcome: Connect gate-level choices to electrical load and timing.
lessons.practical_assignment: Analyze and simulate an inverter chain or compare library-cell drive strengths under several loads. Pass: assumptions are stated, input loading is included and model predictions are compared with available characterized or simulated results.
lessons.assigned_reading: R49: CMOS devices, combinational circuits and delay; R30: MOS circuit foundations.

lessons.title: Static timing analysis, clocks and timing exceptions
lessons.outcome: Check every required path under the correct timing contract.
lessons.practical_assignment: Constrain a small sequential block and inspect worst setup and hold paths. Pass: no unexplained unconstrained endpoints, every exception is justified and a deliberately tightened clock produces an understood violation.
lessons.assigned_reading: R39: timing analysis and flow constraints; R49: sequential timing and clocking.

lessons.title: Synthesis, placement, clock trees, routing and physical checks
lessons.outcome: Understand how a logical netlist becomes a physical layout.
lessons.practical_assignment: Run a small block through an educational OpenROAD-compatible flow or inspect a provided open example. Pass: capture stage reports, identify a routing/timing change and state which physical checks were and were not performed.
lessons.assigned_reading: R39: flow stages, placement, clock tree and routing; R49: physical-design methodology and EDA.

lessons.title: Power, area, process corners and design-space closure
lessons.outcome: Report PPA with enough assumptions to make comparison meaningful.
lessons.practical_assignment: Compare two verified RTL implementations using identical flow assumptions. Pass: report area, worst timing and activity-based power estimates where supported, with uncertainty and no unsupported commercial-silicon claim.
lessons.assigned_reading: R49: power, timing and implementation tradeoffs; R39: reports and analysis; R30: energy and electrical models.

modules.title: Verification, reliability and hardware trust boundaries
modules.project: Create a verification dossier for the hardware capstone: requirements-to-tests traceability, assertions, coverage, clock/reset review, fault injection and a clearly bounded assurance claim.

lessons.title: Formal properties, abstraction and assume-guarantee reasoning
lessons.outcome: Prove useful properties without hiding failures in assumptions.
lessons.practical_assignment: Prove a queue, arbiter or transaction property and inject a violation. Pass: assumptions are reviewed independently, contention is covered and bounded, proven, failed and unknown results are reported separately.
lessons.assigned_reading: R50: safety, liveness, induction, cover and assumptions; R49: verification methodology.

lessons.title: Clock/reset crossings and asynchronous FIFO verification
lessons.outcome: Check digital protocol correctness while acknowledging analog risk.
lessons.practical_assignment: Model an asynchronous FIFO or event handshake with independent clocks and reset sequences. Pass: no loss/duplication under the stated protocol, full/empty behavior is checked and physical synchronizer assumptions are listed separately.
lessons.assigned_reading: R50: multiclock modeling and verification; R49: sequential circuits and synchronization; revisit Module 32 timing boundaries.

lessons.title: Fault models, ECC, testability and recovery
lessons.outcome: Design for detectable failures rather than assuming perfect hardware.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement a parity and a small single-error-correcting code model, then inject faults. Pass: enumerate the supported correction/detection claims, test multi-bit counterexamples and define a recovery response.
lessons.assigned_reading: R49: testing, DFT and reliability context; R51: error detection/correction reporting concepts; R06: coding and combinatorial reasoning extension.

lessons.title: Hardware security, thermal limits and assurance review
lessons.outcome: Include isolation and failure containment in the design contract.
lessons.practical_assignment: Write a threat-and-failure review for the accelerator and test malformed descriptors, denied access and reset under load in simulation. Pass: isolation limits, protection assumptions and unresolved risks are explicit; no unauthorized target testing occurs.
lessons.assigned_reading: R51: device access, DMA and isolation; R49: implementation and verification; R50: enforceable protocol properties.

modules.title: Master's thesis: proposal, implementation and evaluation
modules.prerequisites: Gate I and relevant advanced-track modules; independent technical mentorship strongly recommended.
modules.project: Prepare and execute a thesis-scale project in one primary specialization. Budget 400-800 focused hours as a planning range, with scope adjusted through review. The deliverable is a defensible contribution and reproducible artifact, not a promise of publication.

lessons.title: Question selection, literature map and thesis scope
lessons.outcome: Turn a broad interest into a falsifiable, feasible research question.
lessons.practical_assignment: Write a 3-5 page proposal with a research question, 8-15 relevant sources, baseline plan, constraints and exclusions. Pass: a reviewer can explain what observation would weaken or refute the main hypothesis.
lessons.assigned_reading: Use Module 41's paper method and the chosen track's original papers; R44, R48, R49 or R55 are starting anchors, not a substitute for the literature search.

lessons.title: Proposal review, baselines and risk-reduction milestones
lessons.outcome: Make failure cheap before the expensive implementation phase.
lessons.practical_assignment: Deliver a running baseline, risk register and milestone plan. Pass: the primary metric can be measured, a small feasibility experiment exists and each major risk has a mitigation or explicit acceptance decision.
lessons.assigned_reading: R49: project milestone and reporting structure; Module 41: experimental design; chosen method's primary documentation.

lessons.title: Implementation, ablations and controlled evaluation
lessons.outcome: Execute the study without changing the question to fit a favorable result.
lessons.practical_assignment: Run the approved evaluation with baselines, at least one ablation and one sensitivity study. Pass: scripts regenerate results, failed cases remain visible and claims use the preregistered primary metric or clearly disclose deviations.
lessons.assigned_reading: R09 and Module 41: uncertainty; chosen track's original methods and implementation references; handbook experiment manifest.

lessons.title: Thesis writing, reproducibility and contribution boundaries
lessons.outcome: Write a technical argument another engineer can audit.
lessons.practical_assignment: Produce a thesis-style report, typically 30-60 pages plus appendices as a planning guide, and a complete artifact package. Pass: a reviewer traces five major claims to evidence and reproduces the central table or experiment.
lessons.assigned_reading: R49: final project reports; chosen original papers for reporting comparisons; handbook thesis outline and evidence checklist.

modules.title: Thesis defense, professional practice and continued development
modules.prerequisites: Module 49 and all prerequisites for the selected specialization.
modules.project: Gate J: defend the thesis, pass an independent artifact reproduction, complete a maintainable handoff and publish an honest portfolio where rights permit. This completes the self-study program, not an accredited degree.

lessons.title: Oral defense and independent artifact reproduction
lessons.outcome: Show that the learner owns the reasoning and implementation.
lessons.practical_assignment: Hold a 30-45 minute technical defense with a qualified reviewer or peer panel and a separate artifact run. Pass: the central result is reproduced, major questions receive evidence-based answers and required revisions are completed.
lessons.assigned_reading: R49: design-project evaluation as a reference; handbook defense questions and rubric.

lessons.title: Mature-codebase integration, review and maintainable contributions
lessons.outcome: Transfer a prototype into an engineering environment with other owners.
lessons.practical_assignment: Integrate one tested improvement into a mature open codebase or a maintained local fork. Pass: a focused patch, regression test, design rationale and reviewer response are included, whether or not an upstream project accepts it.
lessons.assigned_reading: R05: distributed workflows and contributing; R11: interfaces and maintenance; R26: mature-engine comparison where authorized.

lessons.title: Portfolio, technical interviews and role-specific evidence
lessons.outcome: Present concrete engineering competence without inflated claims.
lessons.practical_assignment: Prepare three portfolio case studies and complete one systems, one algorithm and one specialization mock interview. Pass: every claimed result is supported by an artifact and assistance or third-party contributions are clearly attributed.
lessons.assigned_reading: R01-R02: breadth review; R11: engineering explanation and contracts; handbook role map and portfolio template.

lessons.title: Long-term learning, maintenance and final handoff
lessons.outcome: Keep the knowledge and artifacts useful after the course ends.
lessons.practical_assignment: Complete Gate J: archive the thesis artifact, produce a maintainer handoff and write a 90-day learning plan with one primary gap and one real contribution goal. Pass: another person can locate, build and understand the project without the author's machine.
lessons.assigned_reading: R05: maintenance workflows; R01-R02: periodic breadth review; current official documentation for the selected tools when an update is undertaken.

checkpoints.title: a complete first game
checkpoints.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 1.** Build a terminal grid or resource game with a clear initial state, commands, valid/invalid input behavior, a success/failure condition and restart. Keep the simulation separate from display. Use the included game as a reference, then implement meaningful changes rather than submitting it unchanged.

Deliver the source, README, a rule specification, at least 12 learner-written tests, a saved input sequence and its expected final state, and a short journal explaining two bugs. Include tests for boundaries, blocked movement, invalid commands, restart and repeated rendering without state changes. Replaying the same inputs in the pinned environment must produce the expected result. A second person should run a complete loop from the README.

The oral check asks the learner to change one rule, predict affected tests and repair the implementation. Passing does not require graphics. Do not add networking, a database or a large engine merely to make the project look advanced.

checkpoints.title: a game-mathematics notebook
checkpoints.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 2.** Produce a versioned notebook or scripts plus written derivations. Required artifacts are a logic/invariant proof, vector and matrix operations, a transform-chain example, a one-dimensional dynamics model, a sampling/aliasing demonstration and a small statistically analyzed experiment.

Tests must include a known transform, a zero-vector edge case, an analytic motion comparison, a timestep refinement study and a probability calculation checked by simulation. Show units and numerical tolerances. Do not normalize a zero vector silently or treat a random experiment as proof. Complete and log the required source problem sets.

The oral check supplies a changed coordinate convention, a new timestep and a misleading average. The learner must explain what changes and what remains invariant. A screenshot of a plot without derivation or reproducible data is insufficient.

checkpoints.title: native simulation and a tiny language
checkpoints.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 3.** Implement the core simulation in C++ with explicit ownership and a build system, then add a small expression language or bytecode interpreter. It may evaluate movement or material expressions; it must have a specified grammar, type/error behavior and resource limits.

Deliver a clean build, tests, memory/lifetime checks available on the toolchain, a complexity analysis and a comparison of two appropriate data structures. Include empty input, malformed tokens, invalid bytecode or expressions, lifetime boundaries, container invalidation and numerical limits. Add the C-language bridge for the hardware direction.

The oral check includes one pointer/lifetime defect, a data-structure choice and a new grammar case. The learner should explain the entire compile/link/run path. A library may supply support utilities, but not replace the central learning implementation without an explicit comparison exercise.

checkpoints.title: a defensible systems application
checkpoints.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 4.** Build a local job-based application that reads validated work, performs bounded processing and stores results. A small local client/server or task-processing tool is enough; public deployment is unnecessary.

Deliver a requirements sheet, architectural decision record, thread/resource ownership map, protocol/schema, threat model, automated build/test script, dependency inventory and recovery report. Test malformed messages, duplicate requests, cancellation, partial writes, worker failure and shutdown under load. Run relevant memory/concurrency diagnostics where supported and record their limitations.

The oral check asks why the design is race-free under its stated model, how retries avoid duplicated durable effects and what evidence identifies the measured bottleneck. A functioning happy path alone does not pass.

checkpoints.title: a small 3D engine
checkpoints.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 5.** Build an engine demonstration containing a CPU reference renderer, one supported GPU backend where available, a fixed-step simulation, explicit entity/resource ownership, an asset cooker, an inspector and versioned save/load. A software-only execution path is acceptable while GPU access is unavailable, but untested GPU claims must remain excluded.

Deliver a fixed scene, source assets with provenance, build/cook commands, validation logs, headless tests, screenshot or image-difference evidence, frame-time data and a peak-memory report. The budget is chosen for the declared test machine; 60 fps is an example target, not a universal pass requirement. Test near-plane crossing, resize/minimize, stale handles, malformed assets and resource shutdown.

A second person must build from a clean checkout or extracted source tree. The learner must explain one CPU/GPU dependency and one quality/performance tradeoff. Using an existing engine for comparison is encouraged; using it in place of the central engine implementation changes the learning objective and needs a separate implementation project.

checkpoints.title: undergraduate software capstone
checkpoints.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 6.** Release a small original game built on the engine. Include one finished gameplay loop; collision/physics; animation or articulated motion; bounded audio; an inspectable AI behavior; settings; save/load; and a tested package. The multiplayer requirement can be a separate local two-client demonstration with delay, loss and replay tests rather than a public online service.

Evidence includes a compatibility matrix, remappable controls, readable interface tests, alternative presentation for a critical audio cue, pseudo-localization, a clean-folder launch and a technical postmortem. Preserve CPU/GPU or software-renderer timing boundaries, raw frame distributions and memory measurements. Test interrupted saves, invalid mods if modding is exposed, controller/device absence and exit during loading.

A reviewer must finish the loop, reproduce a bug test and observe a live change. The quality bar is a coherent, testable small system. It is not commercial art quality, a large open world or a revenue target.

checkpoints.title: undergraduate digital-design capstone
checkpoints.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 7.** Implement one RTL subsystem: a synchronous queue with a small processor interface, a sprite compositor, a fixed-point vector block or another similarly bounded game-related function. The module-level processor exercise remains required even when the capstone centers on a different block.

Deliver the interface specification, software reference, RTL, automated testbench, directed and randomized cases, assertions, reset review and synthesis reports. Test empty/full, simultaneous operations, backpressure, overflow/rounding and reset while work is pending where applicable. Label simulation, synthesis and physical measurements separately.

No board purchase is required. A board demonstration is optional and follows the safety plan. Passing FPGA operation does not establish ASIC readiness. The oral check asks for a waveform explanation, a nonblocking-assignment trace and setup versus hold reasoning.

checkpoints.title: undergraduate hardware/software co-design capstone
checkpoints.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 8.** Choose one measured engine workload. Compare a competent software baseline with at least two architecture alternatives, implementing one alternative as RTL, a supported simulation model or a bounded analytical prototype with clear limitations.

Required evidence includes workload distributions, numerical-quality limits, host/device ownership, setup and transfer costs, resource/timing estimates, failure handling and a sensitivity analysis. Evaluate small and large workloads and one adverse case. A negative conclusion is acceptable: proving that a software optimization is preferable is valid co-design work.

The review must identify the maximum application benefit, the dominant bottleneck, which results are modeled and which are measured, and what changes under a tighter memory or latency constraint. Do not compare an optimized accelerator against an intentionally weak software baseline.

checkpoints.title: graduate reproduction and extension
checkpoints.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 9.** Select a bounded published or graduate-level method in rendering, simulation, GPU algorithms or compilation. Reconstruct the method, reproduce one central result and add a clearly identified extension, new setting or rigorous failure analysis. The extension need not be globally novel; its relation to prior work must be honest.

Deliver a claim-evidence map, derivation or semantic argument, implementation, independent reference or baseline, raw data, analysis scripts, one ablation and one parameter sensitivity study. Use equal-quality comparisons when quality changes with speed. Report uncertainty at the appropriate trial unit and avoid training/tuning on the final evaluation set without disclosure.

A reviewer should reproduce the main table or result. Unresolved discrepancies must be explained and narrow the claim. This checkpoint is the prerequisite for the thesis, not a replacement for it.

checkpoints.title: thesis, defense and handoff
checkpoints.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 10.** Complete one primary thesis-scale project. Plan roughly 400-800 focused hours within the volume's estimate, but adjust the scope through review rather than treating the hours as a requirement to spend. A 30-60 page thesis-style report plus technical appendices is a useful planning target; evidence quality matters more than length.

Deliver a literature map, reviewed proposal, running baseline, risk register, versioned decisions, final method, tests, evaluation, reproducible artifact and maintainer handoff. Hold a 30-45 minute defense with a qualified reviewer or peer panel, including a derivation, a failed case and a live implementation question. Independently reproduce the central result and complete revisions.

One thesis is enough. The learner need not invent both a new engine and a new GPU. Completion records should say self-study curriculum and describe the actual artifacts, not claim an accredited bachelor's or master's degree.

non_lesson_requirements.title: Prerequisites and sequencing
non_lesson_requirements.text_markdown:
The default sequence is numerical: 01.1 through 50.4. The digits before the decimal identify the module; the final digit identifies its lesson. Each module's opening page states prerequisites. Complete the practical checkpoint at the end of each volume before using its results as a foundation for the next stage.

Mathematics can run in parallel with early programming after Module 02, but the programming prerequisites of individual math labs must still be met. Do not begin advanced graphics without vectors, transforms and the relevant calculus/probability. Do not begin concurrency without memory and lifetime reasoning. Do not begin physical board work before the circuits and safety review. Graduate modules require the undergraduate evidence, not only recognition of terminology.

When a prerequisite is weak, return to its lesson and solve a new problem. Use a prerequisite repair log: missing skill, smallest review source, transfer exercise, result and date. A tutor or peer reviewer can help identify the actual gap. Starting at the beginning is not required for someone who can demonstrate the listed work independently.

non_lesson_requirements.title: Entry diagnostic: locate the starting point
non_lesson_requirements.text_markdown:
Complete these without searching or using AI. This is placement information, not a pass/fail judgment. The answers are in the answer-key appendix under “Entry diagnostic,” separate from the 600 lesson questions.

1. Evaluate 3 + 4 x 2 using ordinary arithmetic precedence.
2. Convert 0.25 seconds to milliseconds.
3. Solve 3x + 2 = 14.
4. Evaluate 2^8.
5. Add vectors (-2,5) and (3,-1).
6. Find the length of vector (3,4).
7. Start at position 4, move right 3, then left 1. What is the final position?
8. For integer values: x=2; y=x+3; x=9. What is y?
9. What values does Python range(1,4) supply?
10. In the list [10,20,30], what is the value at zero-based index 1?
11. A while loop repeats while remaining>0 but never changes remaining or exits. What can go wrong?
12. Evaluate True and False.
13. A door opens at level 5 or above. Give three particularly useful boundary-test levels.
14. A program cannot find a relative filename. What environment fact should be checked first?
15. A program is fast on one input but produces a wrong result on another supported input. Is that an acceptable optimization?

With fewer than five correct answers on questions 1-6, schedule an algebra/trigonometry bridge using OpenStax Precalculus 2e while beginning Volume 1. Start with arithmetic, equations, functions, exponents, coordinate geometry and trigonometry; then retest. Questions 5-6 can also be learned in Module 07. This result must not block the first programming session. [R40]

With fewer than five correct answers on questions 7-12, begin at Lesson 01.1. Strong results can justify moving faster, but not skipping the labs automatically. Questions 13-15 probe engineering habits that should develop throughout the course.

non_lesson_requirements.title: Prior-learning challenge process
non_lesson_requirements.text_markdown:
A self-reported skill list is not enough to skip a volume. Attempt its lesson quizzes without notes, complete the checkpoint artifact or a comparable existing artifact, and explain a new variation to a reviewer. Require the same practical standards as the ordinary route. Record what was assessed and what was not.

For the math volume, the challenge must include a proof, a transform derivation, calculus/ODE reasoning and a probability or statistical interpretation; a multiple-choice vocabulary test is insufficient. For systems, include a lifetime bug, a concurrency argument, a network failure and a measured performance explanation. For digital design, include RTL semantics, interface verification, setup/hold reasoning and an explicit reset policy. Graduate credit within this self-study plan requires research-level evidence, not only professional seniority.

non_lesson_requirements.title: The study loop and assessment rules
non_lesson_requirements.text_markdown:
For each lesson: retrieve prerequisite ideas from memory, read the teaching note, predict the worked example, complete the assigned source study, perform the lab, answer the quiz, then check the key. Save evidence rather than only checking a completion box. Required source readings are identified by R-codes linked in the resource directory. A chapter's explanation does not replace its exercises.

A suggested study block is 60-90 minutes with a break: roughly 10 minutes recall, 20-30 minutes reading/derivation, 25-40 minutes implementation or problems, then a brief journal entry. This is a planning suggestion, not a medical or cognitive prescription. Use a pace and breaks appropriate to the learner.

Each short quiz has three questions scored 0-2 each. Use 0 for absent/incorrect, 1 for partial or unexplained and 2 for correct with reasoning. A formative pass is **5/6 or better**, completed assigned study and the practical pass condition. The questions are deliberately short; they are not psychometrically validated exams or sufficient evidence of degree-level mastery by themselves.

For each missed concept, write the misconception and solve a changed example. Recheck after 24-72 hours when practical. At the end of a module, demonstrate a new input, requirement or failure without following the original walkthrough. An evaluator may accept a different technically sound answer than the key when the assumptions and reasoning are explicit.

non_lesson_requirements.title: Required depth beyond the short quizzes
non_lesson_requirements.text_markdown:
At minimum, each programming/systems module should produce the stated project, **6-10 additional exercises**, and **five new edge or failure cases** beyond copied examples. Every mathematics module should include **12-20 written problems**, at least two derivations or proofs where appropriate, and a computational check. Select problems covering each named reading topic; use official solutions only after an independent attempt.

For graphics and simulation modules, preserve reference images or trajectories, numerical tests, a performance/quality comparison and one failure case. For digital-design modules, include a written interface, directed boundary tests, reproducible randomized tests, assertions, and tool reports appropriate to that module. For each graduate technical module, add **6-10 substantial analytical problems**, a critical reading of at least one original paper or equivalent graduate chapter, and a reproducible experiment with a baseline.

These are minimum planning requirements, not a reason to stop when understanding is incomplete. A mentor may substitute a comparably demanding assignment. Problems should come from the referenced course or book where possible and be logged by source, section and exercise number; this avoids pretending a one-page introduction replaces a semester's mathematical practice.

The mathematics extensions named in Volume 2 mean: R40 for algebra/trigonometry, R41 for multivariable derivatives and constrained differentials, and R42 for the later graduate optimization treatment. Complete the relevant R41 sections before gradient-based graduate work. Use R54 for deeper numerical methods. [R40-R42, R54]

For hardware/firmware direction, add a mandatory C-language bridge after Module 15: compile a small C source file as C, expose a C-compatible interface to C++, document allocation/free ownership, inspect structure layout and test error returns. C and C++ are distinct languages; do not treat compiling C code as C++ as proof of compatibility. Review the chosen compiler's C documentation and the target RTOS examples before Module 36. [R11, R53]

non_lesson_requirements.title: Review rubrics and academic integrity
non_lesson_requirements.text_markdown:
Use this common project rubric, adapted to the project: correctness and requirements 30 points; tests/verification 25; reasoning and design tradeoffs 15; quantitative quality/performance/error analysis 10; reproducibility 10; communication and provenance 10. Suggested pass: **80/100**, with all essential practical checks complete and no unresolved critical defect inside the claimed operating envelope. A high visual-quality score cannot compensate for an unsafe memory interface or a false correctness claim.

For graduate artifacts: contribution/question clarity 10; mathematical or technical rigor 20; implementation correctness 20; evaluation/baselines/uncertainty 25; reproducibility 15; writing and defense 10. Suggested pass: 80/100 plus independent reproduction of the central claim. Publication acceptance and positive results are not required. Clear scope, honest failure analysis and defensible evidence are required.

Use AI as a tutor, reviewer or brainstorming aid, not an unexamined answer source. Predict before asking for code, identify generated sections, check provenance, test outputs and explain the implementation. Never upload private employer code, proprietary SDK material, credentials or other people's personal data without authorization. Supplied starter code is a learning reference; running it does not complete the learner's own project requirements.

non_lesson_requirements.title: Thesis project menu: choose one primary question
non_lesson_requirements.text_markdown:
| Area | Example question | Essential evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rendering | Can a sampling/reconstruction change reduce equal-error time on a defined moving-scene set? | Estimator derivation, reference images, motion failures, total cost and uncertainty. |
| Engine scheduling | Can a bounded scheduling policy reduce p99 frame time during streaming bursts without exceeding memory limits? | Task traces, competent baselines, burst workloads, memory peaks and ablations. |
| Physics | How do timestep, iteration count and compliance affect error and cost in a small deformable simulation? | Equations, gradient/constraint checks, reference solution and sensitivity study. |
| GPU algorithms | Does a compaction or wavefront strategy improve a specified irregular workload after queue overhead? | Work/span reasoning, termination and bounds tests, skewed workloads and end-to-end timings. |
| Accelerator design | Does a verified fixed-point block meet a game-quality tolerance and improve end-to-end latency or energy? | Numerical error, RTL tests/properties, host interface, PPA assumptions and transfer cost. |
| Architecture / compilers | Does a cache, layout or specialization policy improve a stated game-workload family? | Model validation, semantic correctness, held-out workloads and Pareto tradeoffs. |

These are question templates, not claims that the techniques are new or guaranteed to succeed. Review relevant newer research when the project begins. The 2016 XPBD and 2020 ReSTIR references are stable historical anchors for reproduction, not a survey of the latest work. [R44, R55]

non_lesson_requirements.title: Hardware, software and safety policy
non_lesson_requirements.text_markdown:
Start with the computer already available. The first-day Python work and early programming do not require a dedicated GPU, FPGA, oscilloscope, cloud subscription or game-engine license. Use a code editor, a supported Python 3 interpreter and later Git. At Module 11, add a C++20-capable compiler and CMake. Record the actual versions rather than upgrading tools in the middle of a reproducibility experiment. [R04, R05, R11, R12]

At graphics, choose one supported path: Vulkan, native Direct3D 12 on a compatible Windows setup, or Metal on a compatible Apple setup. Check actual device and tutorial capabilities before installation. A moving “latest” tutorial may assume newer features than the learner's device supports. SDL3 examples must use SDL3 APIs rather than mixing SDL2 instructions. Keep the CPU renderer as a reference and fallback. [R21, R22, R24, R25]

CUDA is an optional vendor-specific route, not a requirement for learning GPU algorithms. Use compute shaders or a supported alternative where appropriate, and explicitly limit claims when a GPU is unavailable. Use official platform documentation rather than leaked console SDKs. No supplied lesson grants proprietary access or distribution rights. [R21, R24, R25, R37]

For digital design, begin with supported RTL simulation and synthesis tools such as Verilator, cocotb, Yosys and SymbiYosys; compatibility depends on versions and language features. Board selection should follow the project and toolchain, not precede them. For architecture and physical design, use gem5 and an educational OpenROAD-compatible flow only within their documented model and library scope. [R32-R34, R38, R39, R50]

Physical experiments require a qualified mentor, exact board/peripheral documentation, compatible voltage levels and a low-voltage safety plan. Keep protective mechanisms enabled. Do not open or modify mains power supplies, CRTs, high-energy battery packs or high-voltage equipment. Do not design a first project around mains circuitry. Do not assume a low nominal voltage removes short-circuit or thermal risks. Use reviewed commercial educational boards and approved supplies. Hardware procurement and fabrication are optional extensions, not first-day requirements.

non_lesson_requirements.title: Source use, maintenance and limitations
non_lesson_requirements.text_markdown:
R-codes identify the authoritative reading directory that follows. The lesson teaching notes and quizzes are original instructional synthesis; cited resources provide primary course material, official specifications, author textbooks or original research. Resource descriptions are not claims that every linked page is a complete beginner course. For example, the Python tutorial is a reference for people with some programming familiarity; CS50 Python is the recommended beginner lecture companion. [R03, R04]

Use the source sections named in each lesson, and log the actual chapter and problem numbers studied. Some course sites are historical archives, intentionally chosen for durable foundations. Software documentation is often a moving target. Record a release or access date and use matching documentation. Where an exact page moves, navigate from the organization's official documentation rather than silently replacing it with an unreviewed tutorial.

The source directory was assembled for this edition dated September 28, 2026. It is not a guarantee that every future link, tool feature or licensing term remains unchanged. Original books, papers, software and courses retain their own licenses. They are linked, not included as copied books or bundled proprietary software. All hardware and performance examples must be revalidated for the learner's chosen system.

This curriculum emphasizes essential technical depth for game engines and gaming hardware. It does not replace a university's full general-education requirements, supervised laboratories, formal academic assessment or the specialized mentorship required for production ASIC signoff. Its strength is a coherent sequence of explicit learning outcomes and evidence-producing work, not a credential claim.
